To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) a generative grasp model that uses a view-based representation of a grasp can be trained to grasp novel objects seen from a single viewpoint, (ii) that the model is improved by compressing multiple generative grasp models, and that (iii) autonomous training can be used to further improve the grasp model.
(a) view-based generative grasp models can be compressed and (b) that autonomous training improves grasp performance.
(i) view-based grasp models improve performance; (ii) grasp models can be compressed; (iii) autonomous training is effective.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how to learn better generative models of grasps that can then be used to grasp objects that have not previously been encountered.
learning better generative models, and with using them to improve grasp performance.
how to learn to perform dexterous grasps of novel objects, seen from a single viewpoint, in a manner that is data-efficient and that allows for continual improvement.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the proposed approach is the first to demonstrate reliable, single-view, dexterous grasping of novel, everyday objects, from demonstration, without human supervision.

, with the innovations in this paper deployed, the robot can now reliably learn to grasp dextrously from a single viewpoint, without any human intervention, and without any prior knowledge of the objects to be grasped.
, by combining the technical innovations (i) – (iii) with autonomous training, a significant advance has been made in the problem of learning dexterous single-view grasping.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

, with the proposed innovations, the grasp success of a robot can be increased by 30% or more, with no change in the hardware, and with no additional training data, beyond what is generated by the robot.
we have made progress towards a robot that can learn to grasp dextrously, from a single viewpoint, novel objects.
we show that a robot can learn to grasp dextrously from demonstration, and then, by adding self-generated grasps, can further improve its performance, all in a single view setting.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, with a view-based grasp model, it is now possible to learn generative grasp models from a single viewpoint, and then to use these models to grasp novel objects with dexterity.
it is possible for a dexterous robot to autonomously learn to grasp a variety of objects, and to do so in a manner that generalizes to novel objects.
autonomous training can be a powerful tool for continual improvement of generative grasp modeling.
